criterion_notes.c1: Examines urban municipal water supply services (WSS) across 11 urban local authorities in Zimbabwe, reporting consumer-relevant service access indicators at the council level (water supply coverage among connected properties, percentage of connected properties receiving water regularly, and daily hours of continuity).
criterion_notes.c2: PASSES plain wording (`plain_criterion2_decision: "include"`) / FAILS narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading (`c2_legal_admin_factor: "no"`, excluded as E03). Under the literal plain wording of Criterion 2, the study examines legal, institutional, and administrative/financial arrangements of urban local authorities (including national legal gaps for O&M and service benchmarks, council organizational structure, internal water-account ring-fencing, and procurement autonomy). Under the 2026-10-13 A16 scope clarification, however, the exposure studied and tested against service outcomes is generic utility operation and maintenance (O&M) capacity and physical infrastructure management—an unweighted composite score combining repair workshops, civil/mechanical engineer and artisan staffing ratios, asset registers and SOPs, trucks/excavators/testing tools, HR training policies, internal O&M maintenance budgeting, and invariant national O&M legal provisions—rather than a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access (eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, consumer tariff or cost-recovery access rules, street-level discretion, enforcement, or cross-utility ownership/regulatory structure governing access). Notably, legal provisions had zero cross-council variation ('similar (very poor) for all the local authorities') and could not be analyzed, and internal budget ring-fencing/tariff allocation to O&M is folded into the composite infrastructure-maintenance score rather than examined as a consumer tariff or access rule. Statistical non-significance (p > 0.05) played no role in this judgment.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary empirical data collected from 11 urban local authorities in Zimbabwe between January 2020 and December 2022 via rapid assessment, structured questionnaires to key WSS personnel, key informant interviews, and documentation review, analyzed using quantitative content analysis and Chi-squared cross-tabulations.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports council-level water service availability, regularity, and continuity outcomes: water supply coverage (fraction of connected getting water, 70%–100%), percentage of connected properties getting water regularly (50%–100%), and average continuity of water supply (8–20 hours/day), alongside non-revenue water (27%–64%).
criterion_notes.c5: Unit of analysis and sample (11 purposively selected urban local authorities in Zimbabwe), exposure (composite O&M arrangements score and infrastructure functionality), outcomes (WSS status KPIs), and study design (cross-sectional mixed-methods utility assessment) are clearly identified.

evidence_quotes.quote: This study assessed O&M arrangements and how they are linked to the functionality of key water infrastructure and the status of WSS in eleven urban local authorities in Zimbabwe.

raw_response.exposure: Operation and maintenance (O&M) arrangements for urban water supply infrastructure (composite score averaging legal provisions for O&M, council institutional/workshop structure, engineering and artisan staffing ratios, asset management practices, logistical equipment/tools, internal O&M financing mechanisms, and HR capacity-building policies) and functionality of water treatment and conveyancing infrastructure
raw_response.outcome: Status of urban water supply services (WSS) across councils: water supply coverage (fraction of connected getting water), percentage of connected properties getting water regularly, average continuity of supply (hours/day), and non-revenue water (NRW)
raw_response.population_and_sample: 11 purposively selected urban local authorities (Bindura, Bulawayo, Chegutu, Gweru, Harare, Kariba, Masvingo, Mutare, Rusape, Victoria Falls, and Zvishavane) out of 32 urban local authorities in Zimbabwe (unit of analysis: urban local authority / council)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded as E03 (Wrong exposure) under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification. While the study empirically measures council-level water service coverage, regularity, and daily supply continuity across 11 urban local authorities in Zimbabwe and would be included under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2 (`plain_criterion2_decision: "include"`), its exposure is internal municipal operation and maintenance (O&M) capacity and physical infrastructure management (repair workshops, engineer/plumber staffing, asset registers/SOPs, trucks/excavators/tools, staff training policies, and internal O&M budgeting) aggregated into an overall O&M score. It does not examine a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing household or community service access (such as eligibility screening, documentation/tenure rules, consumer tariff/cost-recovery access rules, discretion, enforcement, or cross-utility ownership/regulatory regimes governing access), and national legal provisions had zero cross-council variation. Null statistical associations (p > 0.05) were not considered in determining eligibility.
raw_response.study_design: Cross-sectional mixed-methods comparative assessment of urban local authorities using structured questionnaires, key informant interviews, rapid assessment, documentation review, quantitative content analysis, and Chi-squared cross-tabulations
